Let's dive into Chapter 3: Everyday Behaviors That Build or Break Trust.
You know, trust isn't something we create with big, dramatic gestures. It's built—or broken—through those small, everyday actions that show people we're reliable, respectful, and that we care. Think of these actions like little deposits or withdrawals in a relationship’s trust account. Every positive step adds to the balance. But every negative move? That drains it.
What if I told you that building trust isn’t about being perfect or doing something extraordinary? It comes down to simple, repeatable habits—things anyone can practice. Here are some of the most powerful:
Speak honestly, even when the truth feels tough. Show respect for others—their ideas, their time, their feelings. Be transparent about your choices and how you make decisions. If you make a mistake, own up to it fast and sincerely. Keep your promises, whether they're big or small. Listen first, before you jump to conclusions or start offering solutions. Make sure everyone understands what's expected, so there are no surprises. And when things go wrong, take responsibility instead of pointing fingers.
Loyalty matters, too. Speak well of people, even when they’re not around. And don’t be afraid to seek feedback or be open to change.
Every one of these habits sends a powerful message: You matter, and you can count on me. With time, these actions create a sense of safety and openness. People feel comfortable sharing ideas, taking risks, and working together.
But let’s be honest—there are behaviors that can quickly erode trust, too. Think about hiding information, being evasive, breaking promises, or missing deadlines without a good reason. Gossiping, speaking negatively about others, blaming instead of owning up, and refusing to listen or adapt—these all chip away at trust.
If you make too many withdrawals from that trust account, soon there’s not much left to work with. Relationships get tense, and it’s hard to move forward.
Now, if you’re in a leadership role, these trust-building behaviors become even more important. People pay attention to what leaders do, not just what they say. When leaders are honest, respectful, and accountable, it sets the tone for everyone. Admitting mistakes and asking for input? That creates a culture where others feel safe to do the same.
It’s important to remember, trust isn’t a one-and-done deal. It needs regular attention—ongoing actions that keep relationships strong. Even the best connections can fade if we get careless or neglectful.
So, what does it look like to build trust in real life? Make a habit of checking in with people and really listening to them. Always follow through on your commitments, no matter how small. Address issues directly and constructively—don’t let them fester. And when someone does something great, celebrate it and give them credit.
Simple, right? But don’t underestimate the impact. Over time, these everyday habits transform relationships, teams, and even whole organizations. Trust becomes the default, not the exception.
